stops.title: The oldest Homo sapiens: Jebel Irhoud
stops.dateNote: Flint tools heated in fires date the fossils to 315,000 years ago, give or take 34,000; a tooth gave 286,000, give or take 32,000. The timeline starts at 300,000 years ago, so the stop sits there.
stops.blurb: At Jebel Irhoud in Morocco, excavators found skulls, jaws and teeth of early humans lying with stone tools. Flint tools that had been heated in fires date them to about 315,000 years ago. Their faces and teeth look much like ours, but the braincase keeps an older, more primitive shape. They are the oldest fossils yet assigned to our species, Homo sapiens.

stops.title: New tools, and stone from far away
stops.dateNote: Argon and uranium-series dates put the earliest Middle Stone Age layers at Olorgesailie between about 320,000 and 295,000 years ago. The timeline starts at 300,000 years ago, so the stop sits there.
stops.blurb: In the Olorgesailie basin of southern Kenya, people made large hand axes for hundreds of thousands of years. By about 320,000 years ago they were making smaller, carefully shaped points instead, the start of what archaeologists call the Middle Stone Age. The basin has no obsidian, a volcanic glass, yet tools there were made from obsidian found 25 to about 90 kilometres away.

stops.title: Not the only humans
stops.dateNote: Each species has its own dates. The map shows the world about 275,000 years ago.
stops.blurb: Homo sapiens shared the world with other kinds of human. Neanderthals lived in Europe and western Asia, and Denisovans further east. In South Africa the small-brained Homo naledi lived between about 335,000 and 236,000 years ago, and the Broken Hill skull from Zambia, of a different lineage, is about 299,000 years old. On Java, Homo erectus lasted until about 110,000 years ago.

stops.title: Many cradles across Africa
stops.dateNote: Florisbad is dated to about 260,000 years ago. For Omo I, 233,000 years ago is a minimum age: the fossil lies below a volcanic ash of that age.
stops.blurb: Jebel Irhoud lies in the far northwest of Africa, but other early fossils with some features like ours come from the south and east. A skull from Florisbad in South Africa is about 260,000 years old, and the Omo I skull from Ethiopia is at least 233,000. Many researchers now think our species took shape across the continent, among groups that split, met and mixed over a long time.
stops.debate: Scerri and colleagues argue that our species formed among many linked populations across Africa, against the older view of one population in one region; the few fossils cannot yet settle it.

stops.title: Early ventures out of Africa
stops.dateNote: Misliya is dated to 194,000 to 177,000 years ago, a date that is disputed. Skhul and Qafzeh fall roughly between 130,000 and 90,000 years ago.
stops.blurb: People of our species left Africa long before the migration that gave rise to most people outside Africa today. A jaw with teeth from Misliya Cave in Israel has been dated to between 194,000 and 177,000 years ago. Burials at Skhul and Qafzeh, also in Israel, date to roughly 130,000 to 90,000 years ago. Ancient DNA suggests an early African group even mixed with Neanderthals.
stops.debate: Sharp and Paces argue that the uranium-series data give the Misliya jaw a minimum age of only about 60,000 to 70,000 years; the excavators defend the older date.

p: For much of the twentieth century, the search for the first members of our species focused on East Africa. The oldest fossils that looked fully modern came from there, and the story was told as if Homo sapiens had appeared in one place at one time. That picture has changed. The oldest fossils now assigned to our species come from Jebel Irhoud in Morocco, about 315,000 years ago. A skull from Florisbad in South Africa is about 260,000 years old. In Ethiopia, the Omo I skull, once dated to about 197,000 years ago, is now known to be at least 233,000 years old. Early fossils with some modern features are spread from one end of Africa to the other.

The dates come from several methods. At Jebel Irhoud, flint tools burnt in ancient fires were dated by thermoluminescence, which measures the energy stored in crystals since they were last heated. At Omo, the fossil lies beneath a layer of volcanic ash. In 2022 a team matched that ash to a large eruption of the Shala volcano in the Ethiopian Rift and dated the eruption, which gave a minimum age for the skull. The fossils do not all look alike. The Jebel Irhoud people had faces like ours but long, low braincases. A rounder braincase seems to have come later. Genetic studies of living Africans also show divisions between populations that go back a very long way.

In 2018 Eleanor Scerri and colleagues argued that our species did not evolve in a single population or region. They pointed to the spread of the fossils, to regional styles of stone tools that lasted a long time, and to climate records showing that habitable areas kept splitting and joining. In this view, groups lived apart for long periods and then met and mixed again, and modern humans are the result of that whole network. A 2021 review of the genetic evidence reached a similar conclusion: no single point in time can yet be identified when our ancestors were confined to one small birthplace. Other researchers still give more weight to a single region. There are very few fossils, so every view rests on thin evidence.

The idea of a single cradle is simple and easy to draw on a map, but the evidence fits a messier story. If our species formed across a whole continent, then the deep roots of every person alive today lie in many parts of Africa at once. It also means that the deep splits between populations in Africa today belong to the same long history.

Most people whose ancestry lies outside Africa descend from a migration that began about 60,000 to 50,000 years ago, told in chapter 2. But it was not the first time people of our species left Africa. Fossils from southwest Asia, and perhaps southern Europe, show earlier ventures. A jaw with teeth found in Misliya Cave in Israel has been dated to between 194,000 and 177,000 years ago. A damaged, incomplete skull from Apidima Cave in southern Greece, dated to more than 210,000 years ago, mixes modern and primitive features. Later, between roughly 130,000 and 90,000 years ago, people buried their dead in the caves of Skhul and Qafzeh in Israel.

The shape of the Misliya jaw and teeth matches Homo sapiens, and the jaw was found with stone tools made by the Levallois method, a way of preparing a stone core so that flakes of a planned shape can be struck from it. At Skhul, uranium-series and electron spin resonance dates on bones and teeth agree with dates on burnt flint, and place the burials between about 135,000 and 100,000 years ago. Neanderthals lived in the same region around the same time, at nearby Tabun. DNA gives another clue. A Neanderthal thigh bone from Germany carries a type of mitochondrial DNA that suggests Neanderthals received genes from an African population some time between about 270,000 and 100,000 years ago.

Each early find has its doubters. Geologists Warren Sharp and James Paces argued that the uranium-series results for the Misliya jaw had been misread and gave only a minimum age of about 60,000 to 70,000 years. The excavators replied and kept their date. The claim for Apidima rests on one incomplete skull. A broader question is what became of these groups. The later migration accounts for nearly all the ancestry of people outside Africa today, so the early groups seem to have died out or been absorbed. No DNA has been recovered from the fossils themselves to test this.

These finds show that leaving Africa was not a single event. Groups of our species moved into southwest Asia and perhaps Europe more than once, and met Neanderthals there. Most of these ventures did not last. They help explain why the later, successful migration found a world where the two kinds of human had already met, and why Neanderthal genomes carry traces of early Africans.
